chapter_theme: What makes a land deserve the name: people and yield that do not fail, resilience under burden and damage, and freedom from hunger, disease and faction. All of it is void if land and ruler are not in accord.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the marks of a land (731-736), its limbs (737), its beauty (738), and its defects (739-740). The final verse undoes the whole list, a move repeated at the close of the fort and army chapters (750, 770).

731.reading: A land is where unfailing yield, worthy people and wealthy people whose wealth does not sink all come together.
731.nuance: The definition opens with who and what gathers in a place, not with territory or borders. A land here is a convergence.

positions.position: விளையுள் stands for the cultivators, தக்கார் for renunciants and brahmins, and செல்வர் for merchants, so the verse lists three kinds of people.
விளையுள் is land itself, fields that do not fail even when rain does.
positions.quote: தள்ளா விளையுள் - மழையில்லாத காலத்தினும் சாவிபோகாத நிலம்.

positions.position: The wealthy who count are those who do not spend their wealth on evil.

732.reading: A land is desirable for its great wealth and yields abundantly because ruin rarely touches it.
732.nuance: The verse names no king. Parimelazhagar lists six calamities and credits their absence to the king's virtue and his might, which is his addition.

733.reading: A land bears burdens that fall on it all at once and still gives its ruler his full due.
733.nuance: நேர்வது suggests consent as well as payment. Parimelazhagar's gloss உடம்பட்டு makes the land a willing payer, not a squeezed one.

positions.position: The burdens are refugees and herds driven from other lands by war, misrule or famine, whom this land absorbs.
positions.quote: பாரங்கள் - மக்கள் தொகுதியும் ஆன் எருமை முதலிய விலங்குத் தொகுதியும்.

positions.position: The burdens are the land's own, the extra exactions laid on subjects beyond the fixed tax.

734.reading: A land is one that goes on without severe hunger, unceasing disease or destructive enemies coming to it.
734.nuance: சேரா answers சேர்வது in 731. The chapter defines a land by what gathers in it and then by what does not. Each ill also carries an intensifier, so the verse excludes the crushing forms and not all hardship.

735.reading: A land is free of many factions, of ruinous enemies within, and of murderous marauders who harass the king.
735.nuance: Parimelazhagar says the factions are united by caste or by god, a striking gloss on பல்குழு, and his 'enemies within' include robbers, slanderers and even wild animals. Chapter 89 uses உட்பகை much more intimately.

736.reading: The foremost of lands is one that does not know ruin, and whose richness does not fall even if ruin comes.
736.nuance: The verse does not rest on safety alone. It adds a second test for after the first has failed, so the highest praise goes to resilience. The commentators disagree about the ruin: Parimelazhagar means enemies, Manakkudavar pests and storms.

737.reading: The limbs of a land are the two waters, a well-placed hill, the water that comes from it, and a strong fort.
737.nuance: Three of the four limbs involve water or its source, and the fort comes last. Parimelazhagar's hill stores rain and releases it in summer, a piece of water reasoning.

positions.position: The two waters are ground water and surface water, and வருபுனல் is what flows down from the hill.
positions.quote: 'கீழ் நீர், மேல் நீர்' எனப்பட்ட தன்கண் நீரும்

positions.position: The two waters are river and sea, and வருபுனல் is rain.

738.reading: Freedom from disease, wealth, yield, happiness and protection: these five, they say, are a land's ornaments.
738.nuance: Health stands ahead of wealth. Calling these ornaments rather than foundations is odd, and Parimelazhagar's explanation is that such beauty makes people of other lands desire it.

739.reading: They call those lands whose riches need no seeking; lands that give riches only when sought are no lands.
739.nuance: The verse puns on நாடு as land and as seek. The verdict is on the land, not on the person who toils, but it still sits awkwardly with a text that honours labour. Parimelazhagar treats seeking as hardship, and the verse does not say no work at all is done.

740.reading: Even with all these attained, a land is without use if it has no accord with its king.
740.nuance: After nine verses of conditions, the tenth makes them insufficient.

positions.position: வேந்து அமைவு is mutual: the people's love for the king and his grace toward them.
positions.quote: குடிகள் அவன்மாட்டு அன்புடையராதலும், அவன்தான் இவர்மாட்டு அருளுடையனாதலும் அடங்கின.

positions.position: The requirement falls on the king, who must himself be of good character.
The point is the absence of good government.

links.note: 739 says a land that makes you labour for riches is no land. 619 says bodily labour pays its wage even where the divine does not help. The ideal of the place and the ethic of the person pull in opposite directions.

545 says rain and crops gather in the just king's land. 732 doesn't mention a king, but Parimelazhagar reads the absence of calamity through the king's virtue, which turns the land's fertility into evidence about its ruler.

The same closing move in two chapters: a land with every excellence is useless without accord with its king, and a fort with every excellence is useless without people who can act. Material conditions are never allowed to be sufficient.

source_issues: 734: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is a copy of 733's (பொறை ஒருங்கு ...). His விளக்கம் does address 734, so only that part was used.
